To the BST260 Teaching Team,

For my first research question, I plan to use the NHANES to determine how physical activity and sleep behavior are associated with depression among adults aged (20-29), 
(30-39), and (40-49). I then plan to analyze whether there are any observable trends in these impactful covariates between age groups to gain more  information on how 
depression could potentially manifest throughout adulthood. This could help inform decision-making forquarto::quarto_render("vignettes/proposal.qmd" clinicians and the adults themselves in their lifestyle choices, or at the  very least make them aware of the impact their lifestyle has on their likelihood of depression. In the NHANES dataset, depression is  coded as an ordinal categorical outcome,where subjects reported the proportion of time in the last two weeks they experienced feelings of depression  and hopelessness. There are a large portion of NA values for subjects
younger than 18 (because they were not asked the question in the survey), but there are none for adults in the age  ranges I plan to analyze. For my covariates, PhysActive 
measures whether the subject participates in moderate or vigorous physical activity, SleepTrouble measures whether a subject  experiences sleep difficulty, and SleepHrsNight 
measures the amount of sleep a subject gets per night. These three variables have slight missingness, which I will have to determine the pattern of missingness to find an applicable 
imputation method.  I have not considered which specific covariates to analyze yet, but I plan to utilize more lifestyle-oriented variables. For potential confounders, I could 
include gender, socioeconomic status, education, BMI, employment status, and smoking status. I feel these all can be potential confounders for analyzing the effect between physical 
activity and sleep behavior with depression.

For my second research question, I plan to use the RAND corporation data on firearms legislation to analyze policy trends throughout history in Southern vs. Northeastern states
from 2000 onwards. Specifically, I will create line charts to analyze the effect (Restrictive vs. Permissive) and type of change (Implement, Modify, Repeal) to see whether 
Northeastern states truly had differing legislation compared to Southern states. I will utilize Census drawings to determine Northeastern and Southern states. Furthermore, because
states may have differing “legislative inertia” (Bigger/more populous states may pass more/less gun laws), I will look at the proportion of the effect/types instead. Furthermore, 
differing effect/types may also effect subsequent legislature differently. For example, a gun law that was implemented may be swiftly modified or repealed. There are no missing 
values for any of the variables I plan on using. Furthermore, I could fit a regression with the effect as the outcome and the regions as the exposure (expanding the regions to fit
all of the US instead of North vs. South). The dataset does not include much in terms of covariates, but including political composition, population, and population density as 
possible confounders could help with analysis. This analysis can be important in determining how legislative priorities have changed throughout the “Modern Age” of the 2000s, 
where political polarization, rising tensions towards gun control, and comprehensive media coverage may have changed policy implementation. I may also plan to compare this 
behavior to previous years to see if there were changes as well.
